cards.explanation: The answer is those ravaged by famine. Step out to the country and it's the sword. Step into the city and it's famine. Those are the two sights the word gives, side by side. I think this verse is heavy, so I'll let it be heavy.

The answer is True. The word names both prophet and priest, and both travel to a land they do not know. The verse says it about the two of them together. I think that makes it hit even harder, friends.

The word is peace. They hoped for peace, and the prayer says no good has come. They also hoped for a time of healing. What showed up was terror. That's a lot of hoping with nothing to show for it, friends.

The answer is False. The prayer does mention “…the guilt of our fathers…” but it doesn't stop there. Right alongside it comes, “indeed, we have sinned against You.” They own it for themselves, and that's not easy to do.

The answer is His covenant with them. The prayer says, “Remember Your covenant with us; do not break it.” Just before this they say they have sinned against Him, so they're not leaning on a record of their own. They're pointing at the covenant the LORD made with them. That's a solid place to stand when everything else is shaky.
The answer is the LORD their God. The prayer asks, “Is this not by You, O LORD our God?” Then it says, “So we put our hope in You…” When the sky is dry, they know exactly who to look to.

The answer is Moses and Samuel. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and Samuel, a prophet (1 Samuel 3:20). Those are two mighty names, and the LORD says that even if they stood before Him, His heart would not go out to this people. I think that tells us how heavy this moment is.

The answer is False. The answer Jeremiah is given for them starts, “Those destined for death, to death…” It's four different destinations, and not one of them is a safe place. It's a hard line, friends.

The answer is Manasseh, king of Judah and Hezekiah's son. The LORD says He will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem. The text puts his name right there in verse 4, friends.
The answer is True. The LORD says, “You have forsaken Me…” and then, “You have turned your back.” It's two plain lines, and He says them straight to Jerusalem. That's hard to hear, friends.

The word is compassion. The LORD says, “I am weary of showing compassion.” That's a sobering line, and it sits right next to His stretching out His hand against them. I think it's okay to stay quiet over it for a moment.

The answer is those who have not turned from their ways. The LORD says He will bereave and destroy “…My people who have not turned from their ways.” It's about who hasn't turned, and not about where anyone lives. Notice that He still calls them His people.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “I will make their widows more numerous than the sand of the sea.” Nobody could count that on one hand, or on a thousand hands. It's a heavy verse, friends, and I think it's okay to feel that.

The answer is disgrace and humiliation. The text says, “she will be disgraced and humiliated.” That's said of the mother of seven, who will grow faint, breathe her last breath, and whose sun will set while it is still day. This is one of the heaviest lines in the passage, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.
